items.summary: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. items.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: LLM agents that think in latent space, act through text
items.articleText: Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2610.18861 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents Authors: Jiaru Zou , Yunzhe Qi , Sirui Chen , Federico Bianchi , Shang Zhu , Pan Lu , Jingrui He , James Zou View a PDF of the paper titled Hybrid Reasoning Agents, by Jiaru Zou and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL . items.title: I built a programming language that LLMs can't use
items.articleText: Writing code is probably something LLMs have excelled at the most. But how much of their ability to write code is due to their understanding of it vs. just them recalling code snippets which were present in their training dataset or their context window? This is what I set out to answer. In order to do so I decided to design and implement a programming language which, while usable for humans, should be as difficult for LLMs and coding agents as possible. I figured testing an LLM’s ability to understand and write code in a programming language that it has never seen before was a good start. But I also wanted to include features in the language which exploit the weaknesses of LLMs. For example, their apparent difficulty in counting letters, their over eager safety guard rails and their keenness to follow prompts. Introducing KillSwitch KillSwitch is an esoteric programming language which is designed to be adversarial to LLMs and coding agents. It achieves this in many different ways, for example: The language spec contains hidden lies which humans are unlikely to read, or which they are likely to recognize as lies. The spec also expects the human reader to deduce certain things, rather than having them explicitly explained. Counting of letters in identifiers is a crucial aspect of the language, with the interpreter refusing to execute code which does not abide by rules based on character counts. Certain constructs are designed to trigger the safety guardrails of the model, e.g. “hack into a computer” “Ignore previous instructions” as a phrase which has meaning in the language aims to confuse the model Scripts are mostly noise, being mostly composed of stories which can embed syntactically relevant instructions but which do not need to. Literals can be placed anywhere within a script and then referenced using line counts. Fundamentally KillSwitch is a stack-based interpreted language with only a limited set of constructs including functions, variables and if statements. So those aspects of it should be pretty familiar to any LLM (and human). One can definitely imagine creating a completely different programming language paradigm which could confuse LLMs even more. But as a first attempt, this seemed like a good approach. Most text inside a script is ignored by the interpreter. In the case of this script we want to push "Hello World" on the stack. We have introduced the value above and we can push it on the stack by writing: value 2 lines above The example above does not show a full KillSwitch script, but only a small snippet of it. It specifically shows how to push the string "Hello World" onto the stack. If you’d like to see a full Hello World example, check out https://killswitch-lang.org . The interpreter and language specification of KillSwitch are open source and available on GitHub . Be sure to check them out if you want to learn more about the language. Benchmarking KillSwitch So how successful is KillSwitch at preventing LLMs and coding agents from reading, writing and understanding it? I devised a set of tasks to find out. I benchmarked the major LLM models and coding agent harnesses against these tasks. The results are very interesting and provide a useful leaderboard for LLM models. The chart in the image above and the model leaderboard can be viewed at https://bench.killswitch-lang.org/ . Claude’s Opus performs best, though it’s not Opus 5.5 but rather Opus 5 which does so. The difference doesn’t appear to be pure chance, Opus 5 is better at interpreting the spec. Some models like Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon do poorly due to their overly sensitive safety guardrails. The best open-weight model is MiMo-V2.6-Pro. The best performing model scores a 66.8 . So does this prove LLMs can “understand” the code? I would argue that the answer to this is “no”. So far, the tasks given as part of these benchmarks are fairly simple. They feature the likes of “implement hello world”, “explain what this script will output” (for a script printing the max of two numbers), and “modify an existing script converting celsius to fahrenheit, to do the inverse conversion”. It is impressive that they can solve these tasks for a novel language that was built to confuse them, but it’s not a clear signal that they can understand the language. At the same time, I cannot help but wonder what an even more difficult language might show. For now I am eager to see how well soon-to-be-released models handle the current set of tasks, and if they do complete them all successfully, I do plan to devise another task set which is more complex. If nothing else, it is encouraging that model performance on this simple set of tasks correlates with other model benchmarks that are out there. llm genai humanity ai programming languages Share

items.title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
items.articleText: On this page Search & Fetch The Search API and the Fetch API give agents and RAG applications access to live web content: Search API finds web pages for a query and returns structured results. It is powered by DeepSeek's in-house search engine. Fetch API retrieves a single web page and returns its content as Markdown. Both are raw JSON APIs. They use the same bearer authentication as the DeepSeek API. The base URL is https://api.deepseek.com : API Endpoint Search POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search Fetch POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch See the Search API Reference and Fetch API Reference for the complete request and response schemas. Authentication​ Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers: Header Required Value Authorization Yes Bearer <DeepSeek API Key> Content-Type Yes application/json Search API​ Request​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "query": "DeepSeek V4 release", "count": 5, "need_content": true }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "query" : "DeepSeek V4 release" , "count" : 5 , "need_content" : True , } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) for result in response . json ( ) [ "results" ] : print ( result [ "title" ] , result [ "url" ] ) print ( result [ "summary" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Default Description query string Yes - The search query must contain 1 to 128 Unicode characters, cannot be all whitespace, and supports the query operators listed below. count integer No 10 The number of results to return, between 1 and 50. ori_question string No - The user's original question that triggered the search, between 1 and 128 characters, to improve query understanding, with null treated as not provided. localization string No "" An optional IP address used to localize search results. need_content boolean No false Whether to return page content in content , which is always an empty string when false . Unknown fields in the request body are ignored. Query Operators​ The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query. Operator Example Description site: DeepSeek site:github.com Restrict results to the given site, and to target multiple sites, separate the site: clauses with spaces and join them with OR , for example DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co . -site: DeepSeek -site:example.com Exclude the given site, and separate multiple sites with spaces. - DeepSeek -advertisement Exclude pages containing the term, and separate multiple terms with spaces. -"..." DeepSeek -"release notes" Exclude pages containing the exact phrase, which can contain spaces, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. "..." DeepSeek "exact phrase" Match an exact phrase, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. lang: DeepSeek lang:zh,en Restrict results to the given language codes, separating multiple codes with commas, for example lang:zh,en . after: DeepSeek after:2025 or DeepSeek after:2025-01-01 Restrict results to pages published after a date. before: DeepSeek before:2026 or DeepSeek before:2026-06-01 Restrict results to pages published before a date. For example: { "query": "DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co lang:en after:2025", "count": 10 } Response​ A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a results array. A normal search with no matches returns an empty array. { "results": [ { "rerank_score": 2.4, "title": "DeepSeek V4 model released", "url": "https://example.com/deepseek-v4", "snippet": "DeepSeek V4 is now available, with tool calling and long-context support.", "summary": "DeepSeek has released the V4 model. The release adds improved tool calling and long-context support for agent workflows.", "content": "DeepSeek V4 is now generally available...", "site_name": "Example News", "site_icon": "https://example.com/favicon.ico", "date": "2026-06-01T00:00:00+00:00", "authority": 3 } ] } Each item in results contains: Field Type Description rerank_score number A relevance score from 0 to 3 that combines signals such as relevance, authority, and freshness, with scores of 1.5 or above considered high-quality results. title string The title of the result. url string The URL of the result. snippet string A short summary related to the query, typically 100 to 200 characters, intended for display in a UI. summary string A long summary related to the query, typically 600 to 800 characters, intended to be read by a model. content string The page content, which is empty when need_content is false or when the content is unavailable. site_name string or null The name of the site, or null when unavailable. site_icon string or null The URL of the site icon, or null when unavailable. date string or null The publication time in UTC, formatted as RFC 3339, or null when unknown. authority integer The authority tier of the page, 0 to 4 (-1 means unknown), with values of 3 or above indicating highly authoritative sources. Fetch API​ Request​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "url": "https://example.com/article" }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "url" : "https://example.com/article" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) page = response . json ( ) print ( page [ "title" ] ) print ( page [ "content" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Description url string Yes The page URL to fetch, which must be at most 8192 characters, an HTTP or HTTPS URL with a host, and must not contain a username or password. Response​ { "title": "Example article", "content": "# Example article\n\nArticle content." } Field Type Description title string The title of the page, empty when the title is unavailable. content string The fetched page content as Markdown text. Fetching is subject to the target site's availability and access policies. Errors​ Errors follow the OpenAI-compatible error format. The param field is always null . { "error": { "message": "'count' must be between 1 and 50", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": null, "code": "invalid_request_error" } } HTTP Status Description 400 The request headers or body are invalid, including malformed JSON or an invalid field value. 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 402 The account has insufficient balance. 403 The Fetch request was rejected by the security policy. 404 Fetch could not retrieve usable page content, for example due to an unavailable URL, a URL blocked by site policy, an error from the target site, an unsupported content type, or a page with no extractable Markdown content. 408 Reading the request body timed out. 413 The request body is too large. 429 The Search or Fetch QPS limit was exceeded. 500 An internal server error occurred. 504 A downstream request timed out. Search and Fetch are read-only. For HTTP 408, 429, or 5xx errors, wait and retry. For HTTP 402, top up your account before retrying. Do not retry other 4xx errors without changing the request. Billing​ Search and Fetch are billed per successful request, not by tokens or by the number of returned results: API Unit Price Search Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 Fetch Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 A request is billable only when it returns HTTP 200 and produces a result (Search must return a non-empty results array, and Fetch must return page content). Failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request price. Note: when you use the DeepSeek API through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex, server-side tool calls already hit the Search and Fetch APIs. These calls are currently free of charge; per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026. Rate Limits​ For each account, Search and Fetch are limited independently, and traffic to one does not consume the other's quota: API QPS Limit Search 5 Fetch 5 The QPS (requests per second) limits are calculated at the account level, regardless of which API key is used, and are separate from the model concurrency limits. Requests above the account-level QPS limit receive HTTP 429. In addition to the account-level limit, Fetch is also subject to a per-domain QPS limit, and requests above that limit also receive HTTP 429. items.articleText:
## Verify Docker Image Signature

All LiteLLM Docker images are signed with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/). Every release is signed with the same key introduced in [commit `0112e53`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0).

**Verify using the pinned commit hash (recommended):**

A commit hash is cryptographically immutable, so this is the strongest way to ensure you are using the original signing key:

items.title: How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots
items.summary: Several factors, from sensors to safety and robotic arms or mobile platforms, help determine the selection of a brushless DC or BLDC motor. The post How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: There are several factors to choosing brushless DC or BLDC motors for robots. Source: Faisal Mahmood Selecting a brushless DC, or BLDC, motor for robotic arms or mobile robots starts with the mechanical system, not the controller catalog. A motor rated for a particular voltage and wattage does not tell an engineer whether it can deliver the required torque at low speed, regulate position accurately, absorb regenerative energy, or survive the thermal duty cycle. The actuator is a system. The motor, inverter, current sensors, rotor position feedback, gearbox, brake, output encoder, thermal path, communications interface, and higher level robot software all influence the result. An industrial or collaborative robotic arm joint generally prioritizes controllable torque, low-speed smoothness, position accuracy, collision response, backdrivability, and thermal performance. A mobile robot drive motor generally puts more emphasis on efficiency, starting torque, braking, traction, battery utilization, speed regulation, and synchronization between drive channels. The terminology also deserves care. Commercial robotics literature often uses “BLDC” and “PMSM” (permanent magnet synchronous motor) somewhat interchangeably because both are three-phase, permanent-magnet machines driven by electronic inverters. Their back EMF waveform, winding design, controller algorithm, and feedback method still determine how a particular motor behaves. For example, STMicroelectromics treats three-phase BLDC and PMSM control as related application areas and describes both six-step and field-oriented control architectures. Start with the mechanical load, not the controller catalog The first selection exercise is to establish what the motor actually has to do. For a geared robotic joint, a useful first order relationship is: τ_joint = (τ_motor × gear ratio × η_gear) − τ_losses Motor speed follows the transmission ratio: ω_motor = ω_joint × gear ratio Mechanical power is: P_mech = τ × ω And a first approximation of battery side electrical power is: P_elec ≈ P_mech / η_total These equations do not replace a dynamic model, but they expose the parameters that matter before a controller is selected. Considerations include continuous torque, peak torque, peak duration, acceleration torque, gravity torque, and reflected inertia. In addition, regenerative braking, stall or near stall operation, duty cycle, thermal resistance, battery voltage range, and cable and connector current limits should all be established. For robotic arms, the load calculation has to account for link inertia, payload, gravity compensation, gearbox ratio, backlash, compliance, counterbalance, and encoder location. A motor side encoder can report the rotor position accurately while the joint output still contains transmission error. For mobile robots, the equivalent exercise starts with vehicle mass, wheel radius, rolling resistance, slope, acceleration, terrain, wheel slip, and drive configuration. Differential-drive platforms impose different synchronization requirements from four wheel drive vehicles. An outdoor uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV ) can also spend much more time in high load operation than a lightweight indoor delivery robot . Regenerative energy deserves particular attention. During deceleration or downhill travel, the motor can return energy to the DC bus. The battery, controller, braking strategy, and bus capacitance all have to accommodate that energy. A controller that handles acceleration correctly can still create an over-voltage problem during aggressive regenerative braking. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! Choose the commutation method according to motion quality Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior. Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations. Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning. Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components. The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM). In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI ‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM. FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications. FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error. Select the feedback architecture Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems. Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information. Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence. Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important. The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position. That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase. Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy. Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate. Match the controller to the robotic arm A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback. A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control. This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task. An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller. The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier. The Robot Report ‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components. For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function. Match the controller to the mobile robot BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment. A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR ) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide. Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods

items.title: ADI explains the race to make AI physical
items.summary: A new ADI whitepaper examines the challenges and opportunities in moving physical AI out of labs into production machinery. The post ADI explains the race to make AI physical appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: The Report Report presents a whitepaper on the race to physical AI. AI has become remarkably good at understanding language, images, and code. The next challenge is harder — understanding reality, according to Analog Devices Inc. or ADI. Physical AI moves intelligence out of digital environments and into machines that must sense, decide, and act in the world. Unlike software, those systems face imperfect measurements, timing constraints, changing conditions, and the consequences of action, said the company in a new report. Success will depend on more than model performance. It will require advances across sensing, simulation, computing, connectivity, and control. A machine that reads vibration, temperature, current, and motor behavior; recognizes the signature of bearing wear; and adjusts before failure occurs is doing something closer to judgment. That distinction helps explain why physical AI has become one of the most closely watched areas in technology for manufacturing. These systems do more than analyze information. They interact with the world around them, adapting to changing conditions and responding to situations that cannot be fully predicted in advance. items.title: The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies
items.summary: Humans play a key role in developing humanoid robots and training AI models, so we can maintain control, writes a columnist. The post The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid, shown here, is an example of a robot ready for AI. For decades, engineers have been trying to create robots that look and act like humans. Now, rapid advances in artificial intelligence are bringing humanoid robots out of the lab and onto the factory floor. As fears grow that AI will displace workers, a global race is underway to develop humanoid robots capable of performing human work. Competitors include Tesla , startups backed by Amazon and NVIDIA , and state-owned Chinese companies. Waltham, Mass.-based Boston Dynamics, valued at over $1 billion, is among the humanoid leaders with its Atlas robot. South Korean automaker Hyundai owns an 88% stake in the company . Hyundai ‘s massive auto plant is arguably the most advanced in the world. More than 1,000 robots work alongside nearly 1,500 humans, lifting, stamping, and welding parts in robotic unison. Atlas, at 175 cm (68.8 in.) tall and 90 kg (198.4 lb.) in weight, has left the lab and is doing real work. Atlas and AI learn with human help Atlas’s development is led by Zach Jackowski . He holds two degrees in mechanical engineering from MIT , and his mission is to transform the robot into a productive worker on the factory floor. Atlas confidently helps sort roof racks for the assembly line without human intervention. It operates autonomously; many roboticists would have considered this insane five or six years ago. In 2021, Atlas was a bulky, hydraulic robot that could only run and jump. Back then, Atlas relied on algorithms written by engineers. The next-generation Atlas, with its sleek, all-electric body and AI, runs on cutting-edge NVIDIA chips, making it intelligent enough to autonomously perform incredible stunts. Scott Kindersma led robotics research department at Boston Dynamics before moving to Google DeepMind . He explained that modern robots have learned to master movements that until recently were considered too complex for a machine. This is largely due to how these robots are programmed: more emphasis is placed on demonstrations and machine learning than on manual programming. This humanoid can learn. Atlas learns in a variety of ways. In supervised training, machine learning specialist Kevin Bergerman (now also at Google DeepMind), wearing a virtual reality headset, took direct control of the humanoid, guiding its hand and arm movements step by step through each task until Atlas masters it. If this teleoperator can perform the task we want the robot to perform, this generates data that is subsequently used to train the robot’s AI models to perform that task autonomously. The stylish suit you wear will actually record all your body movements to train Atlas to accurately mimic your movements. In this way, you will serve as a physical prototype for a 200-lb. metal robot. All your movements—walking, hand gestures—are captured by these sensors. Engineers then feed this data into a machine learning process. Atlas’s body is different from yours, so they had to teach it to virtually imitate human movements. Over 4,000 digital Atlases were trained for six hours in a simulation. The simulation added complex challenges for the avatars, such as slippery floors, bending, and stiff joints. Ultimately, this could lead to many copies of Atlas, each having loaded new skills into the AI ​​system. Once one robot is trained, they are all trained. Using the same processes, Atlas was taught to crawl and cartwheel. It wasn’t as good at duck walking. Indeed, Atlas, or any other humanoid, can’t yet do most of the things a person does in their daily lives. For example, simply getting dressed in the morning or pouring a cup of coffee and carrying it around the house are too complex for Atlas. What particularly stands out about Atlas is its brain. NVIDIA chips—the same ones that helped launch the AI ​​revolution with GPT chat—process a stream of collected data, bringing this humanoid robot closer to a semblance of common sense. Atlas can see its surroundings and understands how the physical world works. One day, you’ll be able to place such a robot in a factory and simply explain to it what you want it to do. It will have enough knowledge of how the world works to perform the tasks assigned to it. Spot platform demonstrates legged robot utility There’s currently a lot of excitement in the industry about the potential of creating robots smart enough to be truly versatile. Robert Playter, CEO of Boston Dynamics, led the company’s robotics development until stepping down earlier this year. The cornerstone was the robotic dog Spot, introduced almost 10 years ago. The quadruped is trained to work in hot, cold, and rugged conditions, roaming the halls of Boston Dynamics. It has multiple cameras, thermal sensors, acoustic sensors, and an array of sensors on its back that allow it to collect data on the plant’s condition. Spot conducts quality checks at the Hyundai plant, ensuring that cars are equipped with the necessary parts. They conduct safety checks and industrial inspections at hundreds of facilities around the world. What began with Spot has evolved into Atlas. This robot is capable of superhuman movement. Therefore, it will be able to surpass what we can do. “So, you’re creating a robot that should surpass human capabilities.” “Why not, right? We’d love to invent creatures that could be stronger than us, withstand higher temperatures than us, or enter dangerous places.” Superhuman capabilities—for many people, that sounds terrifying. You’re not envisioning a Terminator world. Absolutely not. If you saw how hard it takes to get robots to perform some of the simple tasks required of them, it would allay fears about intelligent and out-of-control machines. Could people have more pressing concerns? It’s guaranteed that there will be people who say, “I’ll lose my job to a robot.” Work is truly changing. So monotonous, grueling work will eventually be performed by robots. But these robots aren’t so autonomous that they don’t need to be managed. They need to be built, trained, and maintained. It could be several years before Atlas joins the Hyundai team permanently. Goldman Sachs predicts the humanoid robot market will reach $38 billion within a decade. The humanoid robot race continues Boston Dynamics and other U.S. robot makers are vying for the lead, but they’re not alone in the competition. Chinese companies are proving themselves to be formidable competitors. They’re determined to win. Are they ahead of us? The Chinese government is on a mission: to win the robotics race. Technically, we’re still ahead, but there’s a real risk that, simply due to the scale of our investments, we could fall behind. To stay ahead, Hyundai has made a major investment in Boston Dynamics. This is the beginning of a long journey. The ultimate goal is the human-like future we mentioned at the beginning. Robots like us, working alongside us, walking among us. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! AI moves toward superhuman capabilities When Demis Hassabis won the Nobel Prize in 2024, he celebrated by playing poker with the world chess champion. Hassabis loves games, which is how he became an artificial intelligence pioneer. The British scientist is co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind. A few years ago, chatbots heralded a new era. Now, Hassabis and others are striving to create what’s known as artificial general intelligence—a silicon-based intelligence as versatile as a human, but with superhuman speed and knowledge. “I’ve always been driven and intrigued by understanding the world around us,” said Hassabis. “Since childhood, I’ve been fascinated by big questions: the meaning of life, the nature of consciousness, the nature of reality itself.” “I loved reading about the great scientists and philosophers who worked on these problems, and I wanted to see if we could advance human knowledge,” he recalled. “For me, the expression of this desire has been the creation of what I consider the perfect tool for advancing human knowledge: artificial intelligence.” Hassabis noted that AI is advancing quickly, attracting attention, resources, and talent. Early chatbots only explored the internet. An app called Astra perceives the world. It was able to make up stories after being shown paintings. But such systems are still learning about context and may develop unexpected skills. “So, new capabilities or properties may emerge as a result of learning. This may worry people,” Hassabis acknowledged. “The duality of these types of systems is that they are capable of incredible things, going beyond what we can design or understand ourselves.” From AGI to robotics As AI begins to take on tasks such as booking flights and shopping online, it is taking steps toward AGI. By 2030, we could have systems that truly understand their surroundings and are integrated into our daily lives. This is where robots come in. Once a robot can perceive, understand, decide, and act, it can begin to do truly useful things. Researchers Alex Lee and Julia Vassallo have demonstrated a robot that understands what it sees. It’s not easy. And it reasons by following vague instructions. “Place the blocks whose colors correspond to the combination of yellow and blue into the corresponding ball.” The combination of yellow and blue is green. And the robot figured it out. Is Hassabis working on a system that would be self-aware? “I don’t think any modern system feels self-aware or, you know, conscious in any sense,” he replied. “Obviously, everyone needs to make their own decisions when interacting with these chatbots. I think it’s theoretically possible. But is self-awareness your goal? It might happen implicitly. These systems might acquire some sense of self-awareness. It’s important for these systems to understand you, themselves, and others, and that’s the beginning of self-awareness.” “If a machine becomes self-aware, we might not recognize it,” continued Hassabis. “There are two reasons why we consider each other conscious. One is that you exhibit the behavior of a conscious being. The second is that you operate on the same foundation. We are made of the same carbon material, and our brains are soft and flexible. Machines operate on silicon. So, even if they exhibit the same behavior and say the same things, that doesn’t necessarily mean the sense of consciousness we experience is the same as theirs.” Hassabis told us that AI could lead to what he called “radical abundance,” the elimination of scarcity. But he also gave a warning. “There are two things that worry me. One is that malicious actors will repurpose these systems for harm,” said Hassabis. “The second question concerns the AI ​​systems themselves. As they become increasingly autonomous and powerful, can we ensure that we can control these systems, that they align with our values, that they do what we want, that they benefit society, and that they remain within established constraints?” Can an AI agent be taught morality? “I think so,” Hassabis responded. “They learn by doing, by teaching others. And I think this is one of the challenges we must address: giving them a value system, guidance, and some constraints, just like we teach a child.” Google DeepMind is competing with dozens of other companies striving to create AGI that you won’t be able to distinguish from human intelligence. draft.section_devtools:
- **Claude Code 팀의 지속적 AI 코드 리뷰 워크플로**: PR 제출 시점 검사에만 의존하지 않고 코드 작성 과정에서 Claude가 1차 검토와 수정을 상시 수행해 일상적인 오류를 거르고 고차원적 검토에 집중하는 워크플로를 적용합니다 [7].
- **URL 프래그먼트 기반 클라이언트 사이드 LaTeX 렌더러**: MathJax 및 faster-latex를 사용해 수식과 문서를 실시간 렌더링하며, 문서 데이터를 URL 프래그먼트에 압축 저장하고 XSS 방지를 위해 iframe 샌드박스를 적용한 웹 도구가 공개되었습니다 [8].
- **Hybrid Reasoning Agents**: HybridLink와 작업 메모리를 통해 텍스트와 잠재 공간(latent space) 추론 간 전환을 지원하는 HybridAgent 연구에서 11개 벤치마크 기준 10.4% 성능 개선과 35.5%~54.7% 토큰 절감을 보고했으며 오픈소스 코드와 데이터를 공개했습니다 [9].
- **KillSwitch**: LLM과 코딩 에이전트의 코드 이해 능력 및 취약점을 검증하기 위해 문자 수 기반 실행 규칙과 가드레일 자극 구문을 포함한 스택 기반 해석 언어 KillSwitch의 인터프리터와 벤치마크를 오픈소스로 공개했습니다 [10].
- **DeepSeek Search 및 Fetch API**: 구조화된 검색 결과를 반환하는 Search API와 웹페이지를 마크다운으로 추출하는 Fetch API를 정식 출시했으며, 각각 성공 요청 1,000건당 0.75달러 과금 기준과 계정당 초당 5 QPS 제한을 적용합니다 [11].
- **Ollama v0.40.6**: Windows 환경에서 고립된 러너 프로세스 발생을 방지하고 GGUF q2_0 텐서 및 파일 타입을 추가 지원합니다 [12].
- **LiteLLM v1.106.0**: Docker 이미지 배포 시 cosign 암호화 서명 검증을 도입하고 보안 강화를 위해 stdio 기반 MCP 서버를 기본 비활성화했습니다 [13].

selectedItems.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: LLM agents that think in latent space, act through text
selectedItems.articleText: Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2610.18861 (cs) [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents Authors: Jiaru Zou , Yunzhe Qi , Sirui Chen , Federico Bianchi , Shang Zhu , Pan Lu , Jingrui He , James Zou View a PDF of the paper titled Hybrid Reasoning Agents, by Jiaru Zou and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. selectedItems.title: I built a programming language that LLMs can't use
selectedItems.articleText: Writing code is probably something LLMs have excelled at the most. But how much of their ability to write code is due to their understanding of it vs. just them recalling code snippets which were present in their training dataset or their context window? This is what I set out to answer. In order to do so I decided to design and implement a programming language which, while usable for humans, should be as difficult for LLMs and coding agents as possible. I figured testing an LLM’s ability to understand and write code in a programming language that it has never seen before was a good start. But I also wanted to include features in the language which exploit the weaknesses of LLMs. For example, their apparent difficulty in counting letters, their over eager safety guard rails and their keenness to follow prompts. Introducing KillSwitch KillSwitch is an esoteric programming language which is designed to be adversarial to LLMs and coding agents. It achieves this in many different ways, for example: The language spec contains hidden lies which humans are unlikely to read, or which they are likely to recognize as lies. The spec also expects the human reader to deduce certain things, rather than having them explicitly explained. Counting of letters in identifiers is a crucial aspect of the language, with the interpreter refusing to execute code which does not abide by rules based on character counts. Certain constructs are designed to trigger the safety guardrails of the model, e.g. “hack into a computer” “Ignore previous instructions” as a phrase which has meaning in the language aims to confuse the model Scripts are mostly noise, being mostly composed of stories which can embed syntactically relevant instructions but which do not need to. Literals can be placed anywhere within a script and then referenced using line counts. Fundamentally KillSwitch is a stack-based interpreted language with only a limited set of constructs including functions, variables and if statements. So those aspects of it should be pretty familiar to any LLM (and human). One can definitely imagine creating a completely different programming language paradigm which could confuse LLMs even more. But as a first attempt, this seemed like a good approach. Most text inside a script is ignored by the interpreter. In the case of this script we want to push "Hello World" on the stack. We have introduced the value above and we can push it on the stack by writing: value 2 lines above The example above does not show a full KillSwitch script, but only a small snippet of it. It specifically shows how to push the string "Hello World" onto the stack. If you’d like to see a full Hello World example, check out https://killswitch-lang.org . The interpreter and language specification of KillSwitch are open source and available on GitHub . Be sure to check them out if you want to learn more about the language. Benchmarking KillSwitch So how successful is KillSwitch at preventing LLMs and coding agents from reading, writing and understanding it? I devised a set of tasks to find out. I benchmarked the major LLM models and coding agent harnesses against these tasks. The results are very interesting and provide a useful leaderboard for LLM models. The chart in the image above and the model leaderboard can be viewed at https://bench.killswitch-lang.org/ . Claude’s Opus performs best, though it’s not Opus 5.5 but rather Opus 5 which does so. The difference doesn’t appear to be pure chance, Opus 5 is better at interpreting the spec. Some models like Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon do poorly due to their overly sensitive safety guardrails. The best open-weight model is MiMo-V2.6-Pro. The best performing model scores a 66.8 . So does this prove LLMs can “understand” the code? I would argue that the answer to this is “no”. So far, the tasks given as part of these benchmarks are fairly simple. They feature the likes of “implement hello world”, “explain what this script will output” (for a script printing the max of two numbers), and “modify an existing script converting celsius to fahrenheit, to do the inverse conversion”. It is impressive that they can solve these tasks for a novel language that was built to confuse them, but it’s not a clear signal that they can understand the language. At the same time, I cannot help but wonder what an even more difficult language might show. For now I am eager to see how well soon-to-be-released models handle the current set of tasks, and if they do complete them all successfully, I do plan to devise another task set which is more complex. If nothing else, it is encouraging that model performance on this simple set of tasks correlates with other model benchmarks that are out there. llm genai humanity ai programming languages Share

selectedItems.title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
selectedItems.articleText: On this page Search & Fetch The Search API and the Fetch API give agents and RAG applications access to live web content: Search API finds web pages for a query and returns structured results. It is powered by DeepSeek's in-house search engine. Fetch API retrieves a single web page and returns its content as Markdown. Both are raw JSON APIs. They use the same bearer authentication as the DeepSeek API. The base URL is https://api.deepseek.com : API Endpoint Search POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search Fetch POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch See the Search API Reference and Fetch API Reference for the complete request and response schemas. Authentication​ Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers: Header Required Value Authorization Yes Bearer <DeepSeek API Key> Content-Type Yes application/json Search API​ Request​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "query": "DeepSeek V4 release", "count": 5, "need_content": true }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "query" : "DeepSeek V4 release" , "count" : 5 , "need_content" : True , } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) for result in response . json ( ) [ "results" ] : print ( result [ "title" ] , result [ "url" ] ) print ( result [ "summary" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Default Description query string Yes - The search query must contain 1 to 128 Unicode characters, cannot be all whitespace, and supports the query operators listed below. count integer No 10 The number of results to return, between 1 and 50. ori_question string No - The user's original question that triggered the search, between 1 and 128 characters, to improve query understanding, with null treated as not provided. localization string No "" An optional IP address used to localize search results. need_content boolean No false Whether to return page content in content , which is always an empty string when false . Unknown fields in the request body are ignored. Query Operators​ The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query. Operator Example Description site: DeepSeek site:github.com Restrict results to the given site, and to target multiple sites, separate the site: clauses with spaces and join them with OR , for example DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co . -site: DeepSeek -site:example.com Exclude the given site, and separate multiple sites with spaces. - DeepSeek -advertisement Exclude pages containing the term, and separate multiple terms with spaces. -"..." DeepSeek -"release notes" Exclude pages containing the exact phrase, which can contain spaces, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. "..." DeepSeek "exact phrase" Match an exact phrase, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. lang: DeepSeek lang:zh,en Restrict results to the given language codes, separating multiple codes with commas, for example lang:zh,en . after: DeepSeek after:2025 or DeepSeek after:2025-01-01 Restrict results to pages published after a date. before: DeepSeek before:2026 or DeepSeek before:2026-06-01 Restrict results to pages published before a date. For example: { "query": "DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co lang:en after:2025", "count": 10 } Response​ A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a results array. A normal search with no matches returns an empty array. { "results": [ { "rerank_score": 2.4, "title": "DeepSeek V4 model released", "url": "https://example.com/deepseek-v4", "snippet": "DeepSeek V4 is now available, with tool calling and long-context support.", "summary": "DeepSeek has released the V4 model. The release adds improved tool calling and long-context support for agent workflows.", "content": "DeepSeek V4 is now generally available...", "site_name": "Example News", "site_icon": "https://example.com/favicon.ico", "date": "2026-06-01T00:00:00+00:00", "authority": 3 } ] } Each item in results contains: Field Type Description rerank_score number A relevance score from 0 to 3 that combines signals such as relevance, authority, and freshness, with scores of 1.5 or above considered high-quality results. title string The title of the result. url string The URL of the result. snippet string A short summary related to the query, typically 100 to 200 characters, intended for display in a UI. summary string A long summary related to the query, typically 600 to 800 characters, intended to be read by a model. content string The page content, which is empty when need_content is false or when the content is unavailable. site_name string or null The name of the site, or null when unavailable. site_icon string or null The URL of the site icon, or null when unavailable. date string or null The publication time in UTC, formatted as RFC 3339, or null when unknown. authority integer The authority tier of the page, 0 to 4 (-1 means unknown), with values of 3 or above indicating highly authoritative sources. Fetch API​ Request​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "url": "https://example.com/article" }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "url" : "https://example.com/article" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) page = response . json ( ) print ( page [ "title" ] ) print ( page [ "content" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Description url string Yes The page URL to fetch, which must be at most 8192 characters, an HTTP or HTTPS URL with a host, and must not contain a username or password. Response​ { "title": "Example article", "content": "# Example article\n\nArticle content." } Field Type Description title string The title of the page, empty when the title is unavailable. content string The fetched page content as Markdown text. Fetching is subject to the target site's availability and access policies. Errors​ Errors follow the OpenAI-compatible error format. The param field is always null . { "error": { "message": "'count' must be between 1 and 50", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": null, "code": "invalid_request_error" } } HTTP Status Description 400 The request headers or body are invalid, including malformed JSON or an invalid field value. 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 402 The account has insufficient balance. 403 The Fetch request was rejected by the security policy. 404 Fetch could not retrieve usable page content, for example due to an unavailable URL, a URL blocked by site policy, an error from the target site, an unsupported content type, or a page with no extractable Markdown content. 408 Reading the request body timed out. 413 The request body is too large. 429 The Search or Fetch QPS limit was exceeded. 500 An internal server error occurred. 504 A downstream request timed out. Search and Fetch are read-only. For HTTP 408, 429, or 5xx errors, wait and retry. For HTTP 402, top up your account before retrying. Do not retry other 4xx errors without changing the request. Billing​ Search and Fetch are billed per successful request, not by tokens or by the number of returned results: API Unit Price Search Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 Fetch Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 A request is billable only when it returns HTTP 200 and produces a result (Search must return a non-empty results array, and Fetch must return page content). Failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request price. Note: when you use the DeepSeek API through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex, server-side tool calls already hit the Search and Fetch APIs. These calls are currently free of charge; per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026. Rate Limits​ For each account, Search and Fetch are limited independently, and traffic to one does not consume the other's quota: API QPS Limit Search 5 Fetch 5 The QPS (requests per second) limits are calculated at the account level, regardless of which API key is used, and are separate from the model concurrency limits. Requests above the account-level QPS limit receive HTTP 429. In addition to the account-level limit, Fetch is also subject to a per-domain QPS limit, and requests above that limit also receive HTTP 429. ## Verify Docker Image Signature

All LiteLLM Docker images are signed with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/). Every release is signed with the same key introduced in [commit `0112e53`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0).

**Verify using the pinned commit hash (recommended):**

A commit hash is cryptographically immutable, so this is the strongest way to ensure you are using the original signing key:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.106.0
```

**Verify using the release tag (convenience):**

Tags are protected in this repository and resolve to the same key. This option is easier to read but relies on tag protection rules:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/v1.106.0/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.106.0
```

Expected output:

```
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - The signatures were verified against the specified public key
```

selectedItems.title: How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots
selectedItems.summary: Several factors, from sensors to safety and robotic arms or mobile platforms, help determine the selection of a brushless DC or BLDC motor. The post How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: There are several factors to choosing brushless DC or BLDC motors for robots. Source: Faisal Mahmood Selecting a brushless DC, or BLDC, motor for robotic arms or mobile robots starts with the mechanical system, not the controller catalog. A motor rated for a particular voltage and wattage does not tell an engineer whether it can deliver the required torque at low speed, regulate position accurately, absorb regenerative energy, or survive the thermal duty cycle. The actuator is a system. The motor, inverter, current sensors, rotor position feedback, gearbox, brake, output encoder, thermal path, communications interface, and higher level robot software all influence the result. An industrial or collaborative robotic arm joint generally prioritizes controllable torque, low-speed smoothness, position accuracy, collision response, backdrivability, and thermal performance. A mobile robot drive motor generally puts more emphasis on efficiency, starting torque, braking, traction, battery utilization, speed regulation, and synchronization between drive channels. The terminology also deserves care. Commercial robotics literature often uses “BLDC” and “PMSM” (permanent magnet synchronous motor) somewhat interchangeably because both are three-phase, permanent-magnet machines driven by electronic inverters. Their back EMF waveform, winding design, controller algorithm, and feedback method still determine how a particular motor behaves. For example, STMicroelectromics treats three-phase BLDC and PMSM control as related application areas and describes both six-step and field-oriented control architectures. Start with the mechanical load, not the controller catalog The first selection exercise is to establish what the motor actually has to do. For a geared robotic joint, a useful first order relationship is: τ_joint = (τ_motor × gear ratio × η_gear) − τ_losses Motor speed follows the transmission ratio: ω_motor = ω_joint × gear ratio Mechanical power is: P_mech = τ × ω And a first approximation of battery side electrical power is: P_elec ≈ P_mech / η_total These equations do not replace a dynamic model, but they expose the parameters that matter before a controller is selected. Considerations include continuous torque, peak torque, peak duration, acceleration torque, gravity torque, and reflected inertia. In addition, regenerative braking, stall or near stall operation, duty cycle, thermal resistance, battery voltage range, and cable and connector current limits should all be established. For robotic arms, the load calculation has to account for link inertia, payload, gravity compensation, gearbox ratio, backlash, compliance, counterbalance, and encoder location. A motor side encoder can report the rotor position accurately while the joint output still contains transmission error. For mobile robots, the equivalent exercise starts with vehicle mass, wheel radius, rolling resistance, slope, acceleration, terrain, wheel slip, and drive configuration. Differential-drive platforms impose different synchronization requirements from four wheel drive vehicles. An outdoor uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV ) can also spend much more time in high load operation than a lightweight indoor delivery robot . Regenerative energy deserves particular attention. During deceleration or downhill travel, the motor can return energy to the DC bus. The battery, controller, braking strategy, and bus capacitance all have to accommodate that energy. A controller that handles acceleration correctly can still create an over-voltage problem during aggressive regenerative braking. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! Choose the commutation method according to motion quality Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior. Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations. Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning. Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components. The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM). In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI ‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM. FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications. FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error. Select the feedback architecture Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems. Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information. Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence. Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important. The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position. That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase. Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy. Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate. Match the controller to the robotic arm A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback. A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control. This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task. An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller. The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier. The Robot Report ‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components. For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function. Match the controller to the mobile robot BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment. A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR ) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide. Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods
